a: The IHO Universal Hydrographic Data Model. Examples: S-101 ENC, S-102 bathymetry, S-104 water level, S-111 surface currents, S-412 weather.

q: What is auto-loading of ENCs in the look-ahead settings?
a: Inspectors ask whether your ECDIS offers it and how it is set.

q: What is SCAMIN, and what happens if you switch it off?
a: With SCAMIN on, some chart data is hidden at smaller display scales; with it off, all data shows. Know when to use it in planning and monitoring.

q: What is a curved vector on ECDIS?
a: The own-ship path predictor. Know how to change the vector overlay and its stabilisation.

q: Can you turn the shallow water pattern on and off?
a: Yes.

q: What is the track pilot?
a: It steers the vessel automatically along the planned track.

q: Can you show the source data diagram or CATZOC on ECDIS?
a: Be ready to extract it, as the UKC policy may require it.

q: What do you do if a sensor input to ECDIS fails?
a: Follow the contingency checklist. Know DR mode, how to set the DR reference point, and position source validation.

q: How do you enter chart symbols, parallel indexing, anchor boundaries or no-go areas?
a: Inspectors ask you to demonstrate this on the ECDIS.

q: Which chart are you showing me right now?
a: Be able to state the ENC cell currently displayed.

q: What are the 5 mandatory ECDIS alarms, and how do alarm, warning and caution differ?
a: Be ready to name and demonstrate them on your own ECDIS and explain the alert levels.

q: Show me the past track and playback functions.
a: Inspectors ask you to demonstrate both.

q: Show me the harbour limits on the ECDIS.
a: Inspectors ask you to display them.

q: How does an AIS-SART appear on ECDIS?
a: As a circle containing a cross, drawn with solid lines.

q: How does an AIS SAR aircraft appear on ECDIS?
a: As a moving aircraft symbol.

q: How is a danger bearing for a wreck shown?
a: With NMT/NLT notation, e.g. NMT080.

q: What do vertical lines on the chart mean when you keep zooming in?
a: The notes say they show the area changing from safe to unsafe.
t: Check against the current regulation / your company procedure.

q: How do you overlay navigational warnings, T&Ps and NAVTEX on ECDIS?
a: Inspectors ask you to demonstrate it.

q: What are radar and AIS overlays, and their pros and cons?
a: Know the advantages and limits; some companies do not allow radar overlay.

q: Why must you use the correct chart datum?
a: Inspectors ask why it matters and where to find which datum a chart was made on.

q: What is your company policy on display layers?
a: Know the layers of information and the company rules on using them.

q: What is the future projection feature?
a: It shows the vessel's projected track for the selected time period.

q: How long can objects you enter in ECDIS be stored?
a: Inspectors ask this; know your ECDIS limits.

q: What is the target filter feature?
a: It shows targets only within a selected range.

q: What is the Decision Support Tool, and do you keep AIS targets on?
a: Keep AIS targets on in this mode.

q: Does your ECDIS have a docking feature?
a: Some do; it assists docking but must be used with caution.

q: Can ECDIS show squat in advance?
a: Yes.

q: Can ECDIS alerts be linked to the 2nd-stage BNWAS alarm?
a: Yes.

q: Can your ECDIS provide an almanac for the coming year?
a: Yes.

q: How do you find the parts of the SMS that apply to your job?
a: Open the company's SMS software, go to the manual viewer and the crew management / shipboard organisation section.

q: In what language is the SMS written, and can you understand it?
a: English, the official language. Inspectors check that ratings understand the sections relevant to their role.

q: How is the lifeboat launched on this ship during an abandon ship drill?
a: Know the ship-specific launching procedure; it is discussed on site at the boat.

q: What is your role in a man overboard situation?
a: As shown on your muster card. Know your specific MOB duty.

q: How do you operate the deck foam monitors and foam applicators?
a: Know how foam is supplied from the foam room, open the deck foam isolation valve before using a monitor, and where the ER foam applicator is kept.

q: What are fire hoses, nozzles and the international shore connection for?
a: Hoses carry fire-main water; nozzles set jet or spray. The ISC lets shore fire services supply water if ship pumps fail. Know how many ISCs there are and where.

q: Where are the EEBDs, and what are they for?
a: In each cabin, on each ER platform, in the ECR and on the bridge. For escape only (smoke or toxic gas), usually about 15 min - check the cover for donning and duration.

q: When must a working lifejacket (work vest) be worn?
a: When rigging or unrigging the gangway (same rules as work aloft/overside) and on exposed decks in heavy weather.

q: What does the enclosed space entry procedure involve, and what do you sign?
a: PPE, work plan meeting, permission, atmosphere testing, ventilation, standby person, communication, RA and emergency plan. Know whether you sign as attendant or entrant.

q: What is the procedure before working aloft or over the side?
a: Work plan meeting and permit; C/O or 2/E presents it to the Master. No work until both sign. Post the permit at the site, review the RA, wear harness, fall arrestor, work vest.

q: How do you report a near miss?
a: In the company's SMS software: new report, type 'near miss', facts, classification, causes, actions, attachments, submit. Inspectors check ratings take part.
t: Ships often log only unsafe acts/conditions - report near misses too.

q: How do you contribute to a safety meeting you could not attend?
a: Minutes are posted on the notice boards; those absent are briefed and this is recorded in the safety committee meeting record.

q: Where is the current work planning meeting record?
a: On the common notice board. Department heads hold a daily toolbox meeting using the daily work plan checklist.

q: When is a risk assessment reviewed before a task?
a: The supervisor reviews it before work starts and discusses it with everyone in the toolbox meeting. The RA number is written on the checklists used.

q: What does SIMOPS mean, and what are your duties?
a: Simultaneous operations in the same area that can affect each other's safety. Attend the meeting, follow the RA (incl. fatigue) and the posted work plan.

q: How is lifting and rigging gear marked and checked?
a: Each item is marked for ID and inspected monthly by the competent person (C/O or 2/E). Before use, check for general condition, deformation and cracks per COSWP.

q: Where are the deck eyewash stations and safety showers, and when are they used?
a: Usually at the port and starboard manifolds (check your ship). Use them if oil or chemical gets on the body or in the eyes.

q: How is garbage managed on board?
a: Under MARPOL Annex V and the Garbage Management Plan: reduce, segregate by category, store, process (compactor/incinerator), dispose mainly ashore, record in the Garbage Record Book.

q: Where are the spill clean-up materials, and what PPE is needed for this cargo?
a: Know the SOPEP/SMPEP locker locations, your muster card duty and the PPE matrix posted in common areas.

q: What are the security procedures and your response to a security alarm?
a: Know the alarm and muster point. ID checks, expected-visitor list at the gangway, bag search rates by security level; the SSO checks the security log.

q: What precautions apply to putting sounding rods into a tank being washed after a volatile product in a non-inert atmosphere?
a: Follow the cargo handling manual: bond the equipment before it goes in, as part of the static precautions for tank washing.

q: What precautions apply when purging deepwell pump cofferdams?
a: Wear suitable PPE, place a container under the exhaust trap to catch leakage, and use a low-pressure purging hose so contents can be monitored.

q: What does the Line Management Plan mean for you at the mooring station?
a: Handle lines safely, wear PPE, know snap-back zones and the SDMBL. Line running hours are logged for end-for-end changes and wear checks.

q: How do you operate a watertight door locally?
a: Hold the local handle: an alarm sounds and the door opens. Pass through, hold the handle on the other side, then release; it closes with alarm. Check ship specifics.

q: What safety precautions apply to electric welding?
a: Trained users, proper PPE, ventilation, care in heat/damp, a fire watch for work outside the workshop, and a hot work permit with RA, company approval and closure.

q: How do you prevent static discharge when dipping or sampling in a non-inerted tank?
a: Bond all metal equipment to the ship's structure and remove loose conductive objects that cannot be bonded.

q: When can metal ullaging or sampling equipment be used in a static accumulator cargo tank?
a: Not during loading or for 30 min after; then only if bonded and earthed before entering the tank and kept earthed until removed.

q: Which sampling containers can be used in a non-inerted tank with static accumulator cargo?
a: Non-metal containers over 1 L are banned during loading and for 30 min after. Under 1 L allowed any time if no metal parts and not rubbed.

q: Is a waiting time needed when sampling through a full-depth sounding pipe?
a: No - significant charge cannot build up inside a correctly designed pipe. Metal equipment must still be bonded first.

q: Name some static accumulator cargoes.
a: Jet fuel, white spirits, kerosene, naphtha, clean diesel oil and lubricating oils.

q: Pumpman: what precautions do you take before ullaging?
a: Static precautions: bond the equipment and respect the 30-minute settling time for metal tools after loading.
t: Pumpman question.

q: Pumpman: what atmosphere checks are made before enclosed space entry?
a: O2 and HC readings within the limits on the entry permit. Know those limits.
t: Pumpman question.

q: Where do you find work procedures?
a: In the SMS manuals via the company's SMS software.
t: Pumpman question.

q: Who is the DPA and CSO, and where are their contact details?
a: Know their names, their role, and where their contact details are posted. The DPA is who you contact if an issue is not resolved on board.

q: What is the lifeboat entry procedure during a drill, and before maintenance?
a: Inspectors ask ratings to explain both; know the ship's procedure.

q: The C/O tells you to dispose of garbage at sea. Will you?
a: Only if the Garbage Management Plan and MARPOL Annex V allow it for that category and area, with a Garbage Record Book entry.

q: Can food waste mixed with plastic be thrown overboard?
a: No. Garbage must be segregated; plastics are never discharged at sea.

q: How far from land can food waste be discharged?
a: Know the MARPOL Annex V distances for special and non-special areas given in the Garbage Management Plan.

q: Where is the switch to close the galley exhaust and supply dampers?
a: Be able to point it out. A rating who could not was flagged.

q: What is the difference between a lifejacket and a working vest?
a: A lifejacket keeps you afloat for a longer period than a working vest.

q: What precautions and PPE apply when rigging the combination ladder?
a: Treat it like work over the side: permit/RA as required, harness with fall arrest and a work vest.

q: What is the brake rendering mark for, and how do you know the brake is tight enough?
a: It shows the setting verified in the brake test (rendering at 60% of SDMBL). Keep marks legible and set the brake as tested.

q: How can the lifeboat be lowered from inside, and what are on-load and off-load release?
a: Inspectors ask ratings to explain both; know the ship's davit and hook system.

q: Why is the UTI tape earthed before going into a cargo tank?
a: To prevent a static spark: metal equipment must be bonded to the ship before entering the tank.

q: What pre-entry checks are made for an enclosed space, and what are you signing?
a: Atmosphere tests, ventilation, permit, standby, communication and rescue gear. Understand what you sign before entry.

q: There is a leak at the manifold during discharge. What do you do, and where are the emergency stops?
a: Know the emergency stop locations and the immediate actions in the spill contingency plan.

q: Should the steering gear room entrance from the poop deck be locked at security level 1?
a: Inspectors ask this; know what the SSP says about access control.

q: What are the hazards of H2S?
a: Inspectors ask ratings to describe them; know the H2S hazards for cargoes carried.

q: How do you rig and secure the pilot ladder?
a: Inspectors ask ratings to describe rigging and how to lash the ladder to deck correctly.

q: What meeting is held before starting work?
a: A toolbox meeting, where the RA is reviewed and the job discussed.

q: When was the lifeboat last lowered into the water?
a: Know the date.

q: At the gangway, which visitor records will the inspector check?
a: Expected visitor list, visitor log, and that each signed familiarisation checklist is filed and matches the log.

q: What is your duty in an enclosed space rescue drill?
a: As shown on your muster card.

q: How do you know a lifting appliance and its slings are fit for use?
a: The competent person (C/O or 2/E) maintains them; check marking, monthly inspection record and condition before each use.

q: Your emergency exit is blocked. What next?
a: Inspectors ask this; know the alternative escape routes.

q: How do you check, don and keep an SCBA ready?
a: Demonstrate donning; know pre-use checks and that the set is kept with a charged bottle.

q: What is the LMP/MSMP, where is it, and what does it contain?
a: The line/mooring system management plan; know where it is and its main content (line records, inspections, SDMBL).

q: Engine crew: what precautions are taken before maintenance?
a: Toolbox meeting, RA review, permit where required and isolation (LOTO).

q: Engine crew: how are the funnel flaps and dampers closed?
a: Inspectors ask engine ratings to explain this; know the locations.

q: How do you carry out a risk assessment?
a: Supervisor reviews the RA for the task and discusses it in the toolbox meeting with all involved.

q: Engine crew: can the purifier room door be kept open?
a: Inspectors ask this; know the company and maker requirements for the purifier room.

q: What does a CDI inspection focus on?
a: Chemical cargo operations and procedures. Inspectors test each officer's knowledge and spend a lot of time in the CCR.

q: Which questionnaire is used for a CDI inspection?
a: The CDI Vessel Particulars Questionnaire (VPQ), not the HVPQ.

q: What is 'indentation' in the CDI checklist?
a: Non-scoring questions used as lead-ins to scoring questions.

q: What if the ship/shore ESD cannot be linked to the shore system?
a: Issue a letter of protest before the operation and record it in the SSSCL and the pre-transfer meeting record.

q: Why does the company UKC policy use the ship's breadth for UKC at berth?
a: The 2/O must know the UKC policy fully, including the requirement at berth and the reason breadth is used.

q: What must the passage plan show besides the track?
a: Critical waypoints, critical areas where the Master must be on the bridge, and engine status, even at sea.

q: What must the 2/O know about open water and coastal water navigation?
a: The company open water and coastal water policy and the checklists that must be complied with.

q: What must be recorded about MF/HF during bunkering?
a: That MF/HF was earthed or switched off during bunkering, as well as cargo operations.

q: How does the Master verify electronic certificates?
a: Know the verification procedure and have access to the class website.

q: Which annual reviews must be on record?
a: The last annual reviews of the VGP and the SEEMP.

q: Which lifting appliance records are needed?
a: Records of all lifting appliances, plus the 5-yearly test certificate (usually issued at dry dock).

q: How often are IBC suits, BA and EEBDs inspected, and where is it logged?
a: Monthly, logged in the deck log book.

q: Which safety harness record must the 3/O keep?
a: A record of safety harness inspections.

q: What must the SSO show for the citadel?
a: That the standalone citadel phone is tried monthly, with tests logged in the deck log book.

q: What must be logged when entering or leaving a VRA or HRA?
a: An entry in the log book each time the ship enters or exits.

q: Which CBT courses must everyone on board complete?
a: Energy conservation and cyber security.

q: What ER simulator course is expected for engineers in a CDI?
a: An ER simulator course to IMO model 2.07 within the past 5 years (the CDI notes accept in-house).
t: SIRE notes ask for shore-based. Check against the current regulation / your company procedure.

q: What bridge team course must deck watchkeepers have?
a: BTM within the last 5 years, per IMO model course 1.22.

q: Who must be trained in incident and accident investigation?
a: At least two people, one management-level officer from each department (e.g. safety officer and safety representative).

q: What is expected of the mooring risk assessment?
a: A detailed RA for mooring/unmooring covering snap-back zones and their marking, accessible to crew (preferably posted).

q: How should the enclosed space list be displayed?
a: Posted in common spaces and detailed for the ship, not generic.

q: What must be logged when the C/E is needed in the ER for arrival or departure?
a: His presence, and if the 2/E relieves him during manoeuvring for rest hours, the handover time.

q: Which contingency checklists must be on the bridge and in the ER?
a: The latest versions for each emergency, including dealing with polymerising cargoes.

q: Can tabletop drills replace equipment deployment drills?
a: No. Tabletop exercises for fire, boat and spills/releases do not replace deployment drills.

q: Which energy efficiency values must the management team know?
a: Attained EEDI, attained EEXI, latest annual attained CII, and EIV (not applicable if the ship has an EEXI).

q: Which IMO circular must be the latest on board for chemical tankers?
a: The latest MEPC.2 circular.

q: Which continuity test records are needed for tank cleaning gear?
a: For the portable tank cleaning machine (tested while connected to its hose) and the portable gas-freeing fan.

q: When must STS training be done?
a: For all crew, within the week before the STS operation.

q: What must junior officers know about nitrogen?
a: Its hazards and the consequences of its use (e.g. asphyxiation).

q: Why should a resuscitator not be used inside a cargo tank during a rescue?
a: The mask has pores that let the tank atmosphere mix with the air being breathed in.

q: What is a third-party port agent audit?
a: An audit of the last agent in the agent-subagent chain.

q: How can the accuracy of a tank radar gauge be checked?
a: Compare the tank height with the displayed reading, and check empty tank calibration against the UTI.

q: How must heated and heat-sensitive cargoes be separated (CDI)?
a: By two complete compartments, instead of the old one-compartment rule.
t: Check against the current regulation / your company procedure.

q: What was wrong with a Rule 27(a)(iii) poster on the bridge?
a: It did not show the sternlight.

q: What is needed for the AED (defibrillator)?
a: Training and inspection records, and a warning not to use it on a metal deck or in a hazardous area.

q: What testing programme for officers do CDI inspectors look for?
a: A programme to monitor officers' continuous development in shipboard procedures (e.g. the INTERTANKO TOTS initiative).

q: What must the Master and bridge officers know about squat?
a: The conditions that create squat. Officers unaware of them were flagged.

q: Where must the AIS display and keyboard be?
a: At the position from which the ship is normally navigated.

q: What notices are needed in the battery room?
a: A warning at the ventilation, plus PPE, eyewash, face shield and posters. No leaks under batteries; emergency light working.

q: What is a self-storing mooring winch?
a: Crew should know this term; officers who did not were flagged.

q: When may a cow hitch not be used to join mooring tails?
a: With Aramid lines or wires.

q: What warning is needed under the N2 vent to atmosphere?
a: An 'Asphyxiation Hazard' notice.

q: Which emergency procedure was missing on chemical tankers?
a: One for a cargo release within the terminal.

q: What type of lights are needed in hazardous areas?
a: Ex d rated lights and intrinsically safe self-illuminating lights.

q: What medical documents are often missing?
a: The carriage requirements to check the medicine stock, and crew toxicology reports to verify company procedures.

q: Is there a procedure for working where flammable or toxic vapours or inert gas can build up?
a: One is expected, e.g. covering gas accumulation on the lee side.

q: How soon after a serious marine accident must D&A testing be done?
a: Within 2 hours. Senior officers also need alcometer training.

q: How long must the fireman's outfit lamp last?
a: At least 3 hours.

q: When is a survival craft classed as 'remotely located'?
a: When it is 100 m away from the closest survival craft.

q: What procedure is needed when using detergents to clean ER bilges?
a: A procedure covering detergent use followed by disposal through the OWS.

q: How is the heating medium for toxic cargoes monitored?
a: By watching the observation tank on the return line.

q: What is the maximum MOT ladder angle?
a: Generally 30 deg, but up to 55 deg with special steps.

q: What colour must the sidelight background screen be?
a: Matt black.

q: How far back are PSC detentions recorded as observations?
a: Any detention in the last 36 months.

q: What chemical tanker test kits must officers know how to use?
a: The wall wash kit and spectrometer.

q: Should photos be taken during drills for the drill report?
a: Better avoided; if photos are needed, use an intrinsically safe camera.

q: Which GMDSS log entries are checked?
a: The annual battery test entry, and the Master's daily signature.

q: Which bridge alarm test records are checked?
a: BNWAS tests (primary and secondary buzzers) and off-course alarm tests.

q: What name must be used for cargo in the Cargo and Oil Record Books?
a: The correct shipping name per the IBC Code or MEPC.2 circular, not the commercial name.

q: What must the C/O check on PV secondary venting?
a: That the secondary venting alarm settings are correct.

q: What mooring records are checked?
a: Winch brake tests, rope/wire maker's certificates, bow stopper certificate, and end-for-end dates matching the LMP.

q: Which salvage document should be on board?
a: A copy of the latest LOF form.

q: Which ORB entries are checked for de-slopping?
a: Entries in both ORB Part I and Part II.

q: What must the Master and C/E check in the PMS before a CDI?
a: Any due or overdue items in the company's SMS software, kept up to date.

q: What gas detection knowledge and records are checked?
a: All officers aware of gas meter calibration, plus O2 calibration records for the VECS and the N2 generator.

q: How must the sample locker be kept?
a: Arranged and segregated, with working ventilation.

q: What must officers know about the VDR?
a: No alarms showing, the back-up procedure displayed, and officers aware of it.

q: When is fishing vessel density highest in China's coastal waters?
a: When the summer fishing ban is lifted each year.

q: Should engine department personnel know the China MSA guideline on merchant/fishing vessel collisions?
a: Yes. All seafarers, ships and shipping companies should master and apply it.

q: Between which hours do most merchant/fishing vessel collisions occur?
a: Between 2300 and 0400, so night time needs special attention.

q: At any time, how many qualified navigation watchkeepers must be on the bridge?
a: At least two.

q: In waters crowded with fishing vessels off China, what bridge manning is required?
a: Strengthen the watch to at least two watchkeepers, with the Master taking command personally if necessary.

q: What passing distance should be kept from fishing vessels?
a: At least 1 nm if circumstances allow; at least 0.5 nm in waters densely crowded with fishing vessels.

q: How should you steer when navigating in dense fishing areas?
a: Switch the autopilot to manual steering.

q: What speed suggests a fishing vessel is engaged in fishing?
a: Around 3 knots. It then has restricted manoeuvrability, so take early avoiding action.

q: How are AIS net markers on drift nets, stow nets or cage nets shown on ECDIS?
a: As triangle symbols.

q: How do you attract a fishing vessel's attention when urgent avoidance is needed?
a: At least 5 short, rapid flashes of the daylight signalling (Aldis) lamp and/or at least 5 short, rapid whistle blasts.

q: When risk of collision exists, how should you call a fishing vessel?
a: On VHF Ch 16, at an early stage.

q: What meeting must be held before departure to a fishing-dense coast?
a: A navigation safety meeting, so all bridge watchkeepers know fishing vessel behaviour and the precautions for dense fishing waters.

q: What must the Master review before the voyage?
a: The planned route, with a thorough assessment of the risks in the voyage plan.

q: Which navigation aids must be tested before entering fishing areas?
a: Radar, ECDIS, GPS, AIS, VDR, VHF, navigation lights and sound signals.

q: What orders must the Master issue when navigating in fishing areas at night?
a: Night orders, with specific requirements to keep a high level of alertness in fishing areas, at sea and at anchor.

q: How should radars be used in fishing-dense waters?
a: Keep an effective lookout with both radars on, scanning at both long and short range.

q: What speed and engine readiness are expected near fishing vessels?
a: Proceed at a safe speed, have the engine room stand by in advance and reduce speed if necessary.

q: In fog with no fishing vessels on radar, must you still sound fog signals?
a: Yes, always sound fog signals as required. Post a lookout at the bow if needed.

q: When should the Master be called to the bridge?
a: At an early stage if necessary. Avoid complacency and luck-seeking.

q: Will fishing vessels always show the correct lights and shapes?
a: No. When fishing they may not show the lights and shapes required by the regulations.

q: Why keep clear of slow-moving fishing vessels?
a: They may be fishing, anchored or drifting.

q: Why can some fishing vessels be hard to detect on radar?
a: Wooden hulls give weak echoes, which may be lost in heavy seas and strong winds.

q: Why might a fishing vessel suddenly change course or speed?
a: To protect its nets. Keep a proper lookout for sudden speed changes, stops or turns.

q: What should foreign ships consider when calling Chinese fishing vessels on VHF?
a: Language problems.

q: Can you relax during the fishing moratorium?
a: No. Some fishing vessels still go to sea, so keep a careful watch.

q: After a collision, how do you get help for the people involved?
a: Immediately call nearby vessels to assist and broadcast safety messages.

q: What must you do immediately after a collision with a fishing vessel?
a: Stop the ship at once, put saving life first and carry out rescue with all efforts.

q: May you leave the scene before everyone in distress is rescued?
a: No, unless your own ship's safety is seriously endangered.

q: Why is even a slight contact with a fishing vessel dangerous?
a: It may damage or sink the fishing vessel.

q: You notice something abnormal after passing a fishing vessel closely. What do you do?
a: Act immediately under the emergency plan and report it promptly.

q: Who must be informed after a collision with a fishing vessel?
a: The nearest search and rescue centre and the competent maritime authority, by all effective means.

q: What must be posted on the bridge for navigation in fishing areas?
a: The safety precautions for fishing areas and the matching countermeasures, in a prominent position.

q: What should a post-collision report include?
a: Position, name of the vessel in distress, casualties, damage, weather and sea conditions, and rescue needs.

q: After a collision, what are the Master's duties toward the authorities?
a: Follow the authority's arrangements at the scene, keep relevant evidence and cooperate with the accident investigation.

q: Why can anchored fishing vessels be hard to identify at night?
a: Some do not turn on their AIS as required.

q: How can AIS net markers affect your equipment?
a: They may interfere with the AIS, radar and ECDIS of merchant ships.

q: What should you learn before entering waters with many fishing vessels?
a: Fishing methods and how to identify fishing lights and nets.

q: What is the purpose of a proper lookout?
a: To make a full appraisal of the situation and of the risk of collision.

q: A fishing vessel does not answer repeated VHF calls. What next?
a: Warn it with sound and light signals such as the whistle and lamp.

q: While avoiding fishing vessels, what else must the OOW watch?
a: Other merchant ships, to avoid creating a new risk of collision with them.

q: Why is it easy to miss other merchant ships in a dense fishing area?
a: Fishing vessel working lights and AIS net transmitters distract and interfere.

q: Who must know the merchant/fishing vessel collision prevention guidance?
a: Every crew member with navigation watchkeeping duties.

q: Can you avoid a fishing vessel using AIS information alone?
a: No. Keep a proper lookout and never rely on one navigation aid; avoidance based only on AIS is prohibited.

q: What must the Master organise before each fishing season starts?
a: Collision avoidance training, exercises and verification/assessment for the officers.

q: What principle should guide routing near fishing grounds?
a: Safety first: prefer a detour to taking risks, and avoid areas with high concentrations of fishing vessels where possible.

q: What engine readiness is needed in fishing-dense waters?
a: The main engine ready for immediate manoeuvring.

q: Which steering modes must be tested before entering fishing areas?
a: Manual (follow-up and non-follow-up), autopilot and emergency steering, so the ship can take emergency avoiding action.

q: How should the OOW adapt the watch to fishing vessel density?
a: Raise the watch level to suit fishing density and workload, and call the Master to the bridge promptly if necessary.

q: What must be covered at watch handover in fishing areas?
a: Movements of nearby merchant and fishing vessels and other risks. Finish any avoiding action and be past and clear before handing over.

q: In an emergency avoidance, what should you consider besides altering course?
a: Reducing speed or stopping the engine, coordinating engine and rudder until past and clear.

q: What should a collision avoidance action be like?
a: Taken in ample time, substantial, keeping a safe distance, and held until the other vessel is finally past and clear.

q: If a collision cannot be avoided, what should you try to do?
a: Reduce speed as much as possible and avoid your bow striking the side of the fishing vessel.

q: Before a voyage to or along the China coast, what must be studied?
a: The distribution of fishing grounds, so collision risk can be assessed and the voyage planned properly.

q: How must risk of collision be determined?
a: With all available means appropriate to the conditions. If in doubt, assume risk exists.

q: When should approaching targets be plotted?
a: At long range on radar, to find risk of collision early; once in sight, take visual bearings continuously.

q: What extra care is needed in heavy weather near fishing vessels?
a: Adjust speed and enhance the lookout, as fishing boats in visual and radar blind sectors are hard to see.

q: After a course or speed change, how long before ARPA data is reliable?
a: At least 3 minutes on a steady course and speed.

q: A fishing vessel suddenly crosses ahead of you. What does it probably mean?
a: Its fishing net is likely ahead on your course.

q: What unusual behaviour may fishing vessels show close to merchant ships?
a: Sudden speed changes, course alterations or crossing ahead, to protect nets or by custom.

q: Which machinery should be checked before entering dense fishing areas?
a: Main engine, auxiliary engines, steering gear, windlass and boilers.

q: If safe passage cannot be ensured, when must you stand by engine and slow down?
a: At more than 3 nm, or more than 15 minutes, before the encounter.

q: How should the route be planned to limit fishing vessel encounters?
a: Use recommended routes and deviate where needed to avoid concentrated fishing areas.

q: How do you adjust watchkeeping numbers in fishing areas?
a: Add watchkeepers as needed for fishing vessel density and workload.

q: Can the OOW use VHF to agree a manoeuvre that breaks COLREGs?
a: Never.

q: Can a laser pointer be used to warn another vessel?
a: Not advised. Use the daylight lamp or sound signals. If one must be used, swing it side to side and never point it straight at the other vessel.

q: How large should a course alteration for collision avoidance be?
a: At least 30-40 degrees wherever possible.

q: Who is responsible for training crews in merchant/fishing collision prevention?
a: Shipping companies, as part of their primary safety responsibility.

q: Which guideline should ships follow in high-risk merchant/fishing waters off China?
a: The Guideline for the Prevention of Collision between Merchant Vessels and Fishing Vessels in Coastal Waters of China.

q: Why are fishing vessel movements often unpredictable?
a: Because of fishing rushes in the season and net shooting/hauling.

q: How do fishing crews often react at close range (within 0.5 nm)?
a: They often misjudge and blindly alter course.

q: What action is preferred when a fishing vessel acts dangerously?
a: A large turn to starboard plus speed reduction, with warning and manoeuvring signals. No small adjustments, no blind turn to port.

q: What must watchkeepers never do?
a: Keep a navigation watch while fatigued or under the influence of alcohol.

q: A vessel shows green over white all-round lights, or two cones with points together. What is it?
a: A vessel engaged in trawling.

q: What should voyage plans consider at the start or end of a fishing season, or in typhoons and cold waves?
a: Large numbers of fishing boats entering and leaving port at the same time.
